paper_metadata.title: Quantum algorithm for stochastic optimal stopping problems with applications in finance

summary: This paper proposes a gate-based quantum least-squares Monte Carlo algorithm for stochastic optimal stopping / American option pricing. The main theoretical result is a runtime improvement from eO(T m^4 (T+m^2) / epsilon^2) classically to eO(T^2 m^3 / epsilon) quantumly, and under smoothness assumptions to eO((5T/epsilon)^(1+4d/n)) quantum versus eO((5T/epsilon)^(2+6d/n)) classical, with the high-smoothness regime approaching eO(1/epsilon) vs eO(1/epsilon^2).

experiments.description: Quantum least-squares Monte Carlo algorithm for stochastic optimal stopping / American option pricing, with case studies for Brownian motion and geometric Brownian motion processes.

algorithm.variant: Quantum LSM using recursive quantum Monte Carlo subroutines

problem_formulation.encoding_details: No QUBO/Ising encoding; the problem is formulated as stochastic optimal stopping with dynamic programming and least-squares regression over basis functions.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Approximate U0 = sup_tau E[Z_tau] for a stochastic process, i.e., the optimal stopping value / American option price.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Stopping rule implemented via recursive comparison of payoff z_t(X_t) and continuation value approximation e_alpha_t · e_t(X_t).

problem_instance.description: Stochastic optimal stopping / American option pricing under a Markov chain model; explicit case studies for Brownian motion and geometric Brownian motion.

dataset_specification.description: Brownian motion and geometric Brownian motion processes; no empirical market dataset used.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Theoretical error and runtime analysis; no numerical benchmark table or empirical run counts reported in the paper text provided.

hardware.framework: standard circuit model / quantum arithmetic model; no specific SDK named

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical linear algebra for matrix inversion eA_t^{-1} and classical post-processing of e_alpha_t = eA_t^{-1} e_b_t
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Construct basis functions; compute/approximate matrices A_t and vectors b_t; prepare quantum oracles for sampling and function evaluation.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Classically invert estimated matrices and compute regression coefficients; output max{Z0, estimated continuation value at t=1}.

results.value: eO(T^2 m^3 / epsilon) up to polylog factors
eO(T m^4 (T+m^2) / epsilon^2) up to polylog factors

classical_baselines.value: eO(T m^4 (T+m^2) / epsilon^2) up to polylog factors

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical least squares monte carlo / classical Monte Carlo subroutines
speedup_claims.conditions: under mild assumptions; in the high-smoothness regime and with quantum Monte Carlo subroutines
speedup_claims.caveats: Speedup is in runtime / oracle-call scaling, not an empirical hardware demonstration. The advantage depends on smoothness of continuation values and on access to quantum sampling/query oracles.

speedup_claims.conditions: when continuation values are n-times differentiable with n = Theta(log(5T/epsilon)/log log(5T/epsilon))
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an asymptotic complexity result up to polylog factors; no numerical benchmark is reported.

speedup_claims.conditions: general theorem with fixed m and quantum Monte Carlo estimation of regression quantities
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper emphasizes that the quantum algorithm requires recursive recomputation of stopping times, leading to O(T^2) time steps.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: eO(T^2 m^4 / epsilon) up to polylog factors in the general theorem; with smoothness assumptions and polynomial basis, eO((5T/epsilon)^{1+4d/n}) and in the high-smoothness regime eO(epsilon^{-1}) up to polylog factors.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: eO(T m^4 (T+m^2) / epsilon^2) up to polylog factors in the general theorem; with smoothness assumptions and polynomial basis, eO((5T/epsilon)^{2+6d/n}) and in the high-smoothness regime eO(epsilon^{-2}) up to polylog factors.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not reported; no empirical crossover analysis is provided.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Quantum sampling access to the Markov chain, quantum query access to payoff/basis functions, and recursive quantum circuits for stopping times; advantage is asymptotic in oracle/time complexity.
limiting_factors: No hardware implementation or benchmark data
Quadratic speedup only in oracle/time complexity
Strong assumptions on quantum sampling and function-query access
Recursive recomputation of stopping times adds O(T^2) structure
Classical matrix inversion and post-processing remain in the loop
Practical data-loading/oracle construction is not addressed

notes: No concrete hardware platform, qubit count, shot count, or transpiled circuit metrics are reported; the paper is a theory paper with algorithmic/runtime analysis only.
num_qubits is not specified in the paper because the algorithm is described at the oracle/circuit-model level rather than as a fixed instance implementation.
The paper reports only theoretical runtime improvements, e.g. eO(T^2 m^3 / epsilon) quantum vs eO(T m^4 (T+m^2) / epsilon^2) classical, and no experimental hardware comparison.
